newsitem.title: BELGIUM: All but Greek to EU citizens on the internet.
newsitem.headline: All but Greek to EU citizens on the internet.

text.p: The Greeks complained that they had to write in English.
One child asked what on earth was going on.
The questions in the first ever internet chat-in between European Culture Commissioner Marcelino Oreja and EU citizens ranged from the irritated to the cheeky, from the confused to the esoteric.
One man named Norman asked the European Commission whether it followed its own rules on the 48-hour week and whether the EU could not do something more fruitful than create a single currency.
"How is the second pillar going to be developed in relation to the agreement concluded in the Dublin summit," asked a more reverent European amateur.

Oreja, surrounded by a roomful of helpers and translators, excitedly answered the questions -- estimated at 60-80 an hour -- and simultaneously translated in the biggest ever multilingual link-up into 10 out of eleven EU languages.

Greek was excluded, raising a protest from Greek Vice President of the European Parliament Georgios Anastassopoulos because it has a different alphabet. EU officials explained software did not exist at present to include it with the others.

The Commission -- joining a trend among prominent policitians like Israeli Premier Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. policians -- to talk to the people on the internet -- staged the event in a bid to bring the 15-nation Union closer to its citizens.
